scenes.name: Downtown: graffiti, punk y hip hop en el Mudd Club, Negril y el Roxy
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Fab 5 Freddy (Fred Brathwaite), del grupo de grafiteros de Brooklyn Fabulous 5 con Lee Quiñones, ofrecía en The Village Voice murales por encargo; con Michael Holman montó la Canal Zone Party (1979), donde apareció Jean-Michel Basquiat, mitad de SAMO, y llevó a Bambaataa al Mudd Club. La Zulu Nation y los Funky 4 + 1, que mezclaban punk y hip hop ante los Beastie Boys, bajaron al Ritz, el Mudd Club, Danceteria, Negril y el Roxy de Kool Lady Blue: en Negril, cedido por el mánager de los Clash, se juntaron por primera vez los cuatro elementos; en el Roxy, una pista de patinaje de la calle 18, Bambaataa, Afrika Islam y Grand Mixer D.ST pinchaban para Bianca Jagger, Warhol, la Rock Steady Crew o Madonna. Debbie Harry y Chris Stein (Blondie), amigos de Flash, nombraron a Freddy y a Flash en «Rapture» (1981), primer rap número 1 en Billboard, y llevaron a los Funky 4 + 1 a Saturday Night Live (14 de febrero de 1981), primera actuación de hip hop en la televisión nacional. Para Holman, sin el abrazo del downtown el hip hop no habría sido lo que fue; para Dante Ross, los negros se llevaron pantalones pitillo y opiáceos y los blancos toda esa cultura.

podcast.title: Singing Career Start (1968)
podcast.body: Debbie Harry's singing career began in 1968 as a backing singer for the folk band The Wind in the Willows, who released one album. "Her singing career started in 1968 when she was a backing singer for a folk band called The Wind in the Willows, who released one album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Artwork Designer
podcast.body: H.R. Giger, known for creating the Xenomorph in the "Alien" movie franchise, also designed album artwork for Debbie Harry. "He did stuff for Emerson Lincoln Palmer, Debra Harry, and the Dead Kennedys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Breakthrough at 33
podcast.body: Debbie Harry became a big rock star in her early 30s. When Blondie's breakthrough record came out in 1978, she was 33 years old, which is considered a long time in the rock world. "It took until she was in her early 30s for Debra Harrya to become a big rock star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Discovery of "The Tide Is High"
podcast.body: While in London, Debbie Harry serendipitously discovered John Holt's song "The Tide Is High" on a compilation tape, which subsequently led to Blondie's decision to record their chart-topping cover. "Debbie Harry heard that song on a compilation tape that she got in London, London and decided that she had to record it."

podcast.title: Early Career Diversity
podcast.body: Before her breakthrough with Blondie, Debbie Harry held various jobs in New York, including secretary at the American office of the BBC, waitress, go-go dancer, and a Playboy bunny at the New York Playboy Club. "She worked in New York. And for a while she was a secretary at the American office of the BBC. After that she was a waitress. She was a go-go dancer. And for a while a playboy bunny slinging cocktails in the New York location of the Playboy Club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joining Blondie at 31
podcast.body: By 1974, Debbie Harry was in The Stilettos, which led to Angel in the Snake, and then Blondie. She was 31 years old when she started playing for the nascent punk scene at CBGB in 1975, which was considered "ancient" for the time. "By the time she started playing for the nascent punks at CBGB she was an ancient 31 years old."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Friends with Blondie and Ramones; Almost Signed to IRS; Influenced B-52s; Background Vocals on Blondie's Autoamerican
xref.body: The B-Girls formed in Toronto in 1977 with a sound closer to British Invasion mid-1960s than hard punk, though their look and attitude were fully punk. They toured with and opened for Teenage Head, the Viletones, and eventually The Clash, then relocated to New York where they became close with Blondie, the Ramones, the Cramps, and the Dead Boys. Members sang background vocals on Blondie's *Autoamerican* (1980), had demos produced by Debbie Harry and Mick Jones of The Clash, and nearly signed with IRS Records — which chose a Los Angeles band called the Go-Go's instead. The Go-Go's were fans of the B-Girls. The B-Girls' existence and sound also influenced a band from Georgia called the B-52s. No album was released before the original lineup fell apart by 1981. "This Canadian punk band influenced not just Blondie and the Go-Go's, but a band visiting New York from Georgia called the B-52s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
